source.title: No regret sample selection with noisy labels
source.authors: Heon Song; Nariaki Mitsuo; Seiichi Uchida; Daiki Suehiro

record.file_problem: Full text provided, including supplementary material.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates standard DNN training on image datasets with symmetric random label corruption and reports test accuracy across corruption rates. It does not measure training error, so it tests only part of V4.
record.gate_note: The Standard baseline's test accuracies across symmetric-noise rates are included. The study does not report its training error on corrupted labels, so these results cannot establish whether it fits them perfectly.
record.test_reason: The Standard baselines test V4's test-error trend under increasing symmetric label noise. The study also reports early generalization followed by later overfitting in its own training curves, bearing on V6. Its sample-selection method's performance alone does not test random-label fitting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct: the authors conclude that TAkS effectively excludes incorrectly labeled samples and offers competitive classification accuracy with lower computational cost. Their stated performance summary is best or second-best in most cases, rather than superiority in every setting.
record.recipe_differences: TAkS alternates DNN training with adaptive k-set sample selection; it is not the original random-label fitting experiment. The Standard baseline trains on the full noisy set.
record.method_sensitivity: Test accuracy varies with dataset and symmetric noise rate; the study reports lower accuracy at higher symmetric-noise rates for the Standard baseline.

fits_no_version.finding: TAkS's selection precision, noise-risk separation, feature visualizations, and computational advantages evaluate its mitigation strategy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive sample selection can preferentially retain clean examples and improve noisy-label learning.

record.problems: The relevant Standard baseline results report test accuracy but not training error. The study averages results over five trials but gives no uncertainty values for these table entries. Clothing1M was run once and has no ground truth for label precision; it is not included in the extracted rows.
record.rows_left_out: No other results on the claim versions are reported. Ablation results compare TAkS with its selection variants, not random-label fitting; other test-accuracy and label-precision results concern sample-selection methods. Figure curves are not separately extracted because Table 1 provides the relevant Standard test-accuracy values.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and fitting without changing architecture or hyperparameters.
Time to fit true versus random labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions. Reported timing compares training methods, not time to achieve a common fitting criterion.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training-set fit at each corruption level; clean-label and fully random-label endpoints; behavior between the three sampled corruption rates.
Effects of adding or removing weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Direct measurement of clean-label versus corrupted-label training accuracy or loss over time, and learning dynamics under completely random labels.

missing.what: The temporal result supporting V6: early test-accuracy peaks followed by rapid declines for Standard, F-correction, and Decouple, interpreted explicitly as general-feature learning followed by overfitting incorrect labels. Endpoint averages cannot represent this result, despite rows_left_out treating the curves as redundant.
missing.locator: Section 5.3, Classification performance; Figure 2; supplementary Section D.2 and Figures 7–9

record.verdict_notes: Observed row states refer only to the measured test-error trend within V4. Corruption replaces selected labels with incorrect alternatives; the experiment includes neither zero corruption nor completely random labeling. The V6 verdict rests on the authors' explicit interpretation of their own temporal results, not merely their citation of Arpit et al.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling, training error, chance test error, unchanged architecture and hyperparameters, and comparison with true-label generalization.
Training time or convergence speed for fitting random labels versus true labels, and its relation to corrupted-label fraction.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, Gaussian-noise inputs, and their training error.
Whether standard training fits the corrupted training labels perfectly; only the symmetric-noise test-accuracy results are extracted.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation affect fitting random labels or true-label generalization.
Whether real patterns are learned before noisy or random labels, or whether those labels are learned differently over training.

relationships.condition: Standard training on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 at 20%, 50%, and 80% symmetric label corruption; test-error component only
relationships.reason: Accuracy falls monotonically: MNIST 78.67→51.22→22.43%, CIFAR-10 68.92→41.93→15.85%, and CIFAR-100 35.51→17.31→4.25% (R1–R9). Missing training-error measurements do not justify limits_scope.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy declined successively to 78.67%, 51.22%, and 22.43% on MNIST; 68.92%, 41.93%, and 15.85% on CIFAR-10; and 35.51%, 17.31%, and 4.25% on CIFAR-100.

relationships.condition: Early versus late training of Standard, F-correction, and Decouple on noisy CIFAR-10, in most reported settings
relationships.reason: Based on Section 5.3 and Figure 2, missing from the rows: test accuracy peaks early and then drops rapidly; the authors interpret this as learning general features before overfitting incorrect labels. This is indirect evidence of the learning order.
relationships.display_finding: Test accuracy usually peaked early and then dropped rapidly, which the authors attributed to learning general features before overfitting incorrect labels.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
